summary_md: Zeileis (JSS 11(10), 2004; reprinted as the sandwich package introduction) is a software paper, not an empirical study. It casts HC and HAC covariance estimators as one sandwich form, (X'X)^-1 X'Omega X (X'X)^-1, and gives R tools that plug into coeftest and structural-change tests: vcovHC (const, HC0-HC4, HC3 default) and vcovHAC with Newey-West, Andrews kernel and Lumley weights, optional VAR prewhitening and automatic bandwidth. Three worked examples carry the numbers. On 50 US states (1979 school spending), the quadratic income term goes from SE 830 (HC0, p .056) to SE 5489 (HC4, p .77) because one high-leverage state, Alaska, drives it. On the Greene investment series, three HAC settings move the RealGNP SE from 0.0168 to 0.0236 (about 40 percent) without changing the conclusion. On quarterly US real interest 1961-1986 (103 quarters), a HAC-scaled CUSUM rejects stability (p .0082) and Bai-Perron dating finds breaks in 1972(3) and 1980(3). There is no simulation evidence. Claims about small-sample performance come from Long and Ervin (2000) and Cribari-Neto (2004). For Paul's systems this is a method source for the robust-variance rows in Mentat. The forecast refit calls sandwich::vcovHC HC1 and vcovCL directly. The SEATS-W weekly test hand-codes a Bartlett Newey-West SE at fixed lags 2, 4 and 8 weeks and labels it secondary. The paper's own examples support that design: HAC lag and prewhitening choices visibly move SEs. Its leverage example qualifies the HC1 rows in small refit regressions (df about 11). Nothing here touches the network, lobbying or influence components.

bearings.paper_claim: HAC = weighted sum of lagged products of estimating functions (eq. 6). In the Investment example the RealGNP SE is 0.0168 (Newey-West lag 4, no prewhitening), 0.0236 (automatic bandwidth plus prewhitening) and 0.0208 (Parzen, VAR(2)). That is about a 40 percent spread from tuning alone, while the substantive conclusion holds.
bearings.system_side: SEATS-W hand-codes the Bartlett Newey-West SE with fixed lags 2, 4 and 8 weeks. Lag pairs are matched within cycle by calendar week, so gaps are never treated as adjacent. It applies an n/(n-p) adjustment with no prewhitening and no automatic bandwidth, reports the SE as secondary with no p-value, and leaves primary inference to a fixed-X moving-block bootstrap with Holm.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's examples are stationary macro series of about 40-100 observations. SEATS-W is one 2022 cycle of weekly shares. A tuning-driven SE spread of about 40 percent supports showing several lags rather than one. It does not validate any particular lag, and the paper offers no coverage evidence at weekly-panel sizes.

bearings.paper_claim: Leverage drives HC choice. On 50 states the quadratic income SE is 830 under HC0 (p .056) and 5489 under HC4 (p .77) because of one leverage point. The paper cites Long and Ervin (2000) for HC3 as best in small samples and makes HC3 the vcovHC default.
bearings.system_side: The refit robustness block prints an HC1 row through sandwich::vcovHC type HC1 next to CR1, CR2 (clubSandwich, Satterthwaite) and a wild cluster restricted bootstrap. A fixture row shows the HC1 SE on 11 residual df.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This applies only to the HC1 row. Cluster rows and the wild bootstrap already carry the small-G burden. With around 11 df and industry-cycle cells that may hold a high-leverage cycle, HC1 can understate SEs relative to HC3 or HC4, so the HC1 row should not be read as the robust answer. The paper has no simulation of its own, and the claim rests on its citations.

bearings.paper_claim: The sandwich form underlies HC SEs (HC0-HC4 differ only in omega_i weights based on residuals and leverage h_i).
bearings.system_side: sgs_estimate hand-codes an HC1 sandwich (n/df) x A X'uu'X A and labels it reference-only. Inference uses a wild sector-cluster restricted bootstrap with Holm, and DESCRIPTIVE tests report only the estimate and the HC1 error.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The system already demotes HC1 to reference. The paper adds only the leverage caveat: for DESCRIPTIVE fits where HC1 is the sole error reported, an HC3 column would be a cheap check. This remains an UNVERIFIED suggestion until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

gaps_exposed: Mentat's robust-variance rows use HC1 throughout, in sandwich::vcovHC in the refit and hand-coded in sgs_estimate. There is no HC3 or HC4 leverage-adjusted row, although the paper shows a single leverage point moving p from .056 to .77 at N=50 and makes HC3 the small-sample default.

SEATS-W HAC uses fixed Bartlett lags 2/4/8 with no prewhitening or data-driven bandwidth (Andrews 1991 or Newey-West 1994). The paper's examples show these choices move SEs by about 40 percent. The secondary-only, no-p labelling already contains the risk, but no automatic-bandwidth row is shown.

No component runs a structural-change test (CUSUM or Bai-Perron) on giving series. The giving forecast assumes stable phase effects across cycles (D-092), and the paper's strucchange workflow is one candidate check. Treat it as exploratory, because giving series have few cycles.
flags: No conflict with brain rules: the paper makes no network, lobbying or influence claims and does not argue for either rejected SNA proposal.

The paper is a software exposition with no Monte Carlo evidence. Any small-sample claim (HC3 or HC4 superiority) comes from Long and Ervin (2000) and Cribari-Neto (2004) and should be cited as such, not to this paper.
Package versions in the reprint (sandwich 3.1-3) match the refit's vendored sandwich 3.1-3 in registry/models.json, so the method source and the code agree on version.
paul_alignment: Paul has no annotated-bibliography entry and no markup for this work (n_annots 0), so there is no takeaway to compare. The system as built already follows the paper's spirit and goes further. HC and HAC errors are reported but kept secondary to cluster and block bootstraps, with Holm adjustment, which is stricter than the paper's coeftest z-tests. The live code shows the paper is a method source, not a stale citation.

related.why: This is the Zeileis 2006 JSS follow-up cited in the paper. It generalizes the sandwich estimators here to any model with estimating functions and bread, which is how vcovHC applies to the refit's lm fits.
This is the clustered-covariance extension of the same package. It adds vcovCL, which the Mentat refit uses for its CR1 rows next to the HC1 row that this paper underlies.
